section.title: The Call of Isaiah
section.sectionRationale: This is the great commissioning vision at the heart of the book's opening movement: Isaiah sees the LORD high and exalted, is undone by his own uncleanness, is cleansed by a coal from the altar, and volunteers for a mission that will harden rather than immediately heal a stubborn people. It is the theological engine behind everything that follows, judgment delayed by mercy, then finally falling, with only a holy stump remaining.
section.thesis: Isaiah's vision of the thrice-holy LORD exposes his own uncleanness and, once cleansed, sends him to proclaim a message that will deepen the very hardness it exposes, until only a remnant, a holy seed, survives the coming devastation.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the vision of the LORD high and exalted; Isaiah's ruin and cleansing; the commissioning, here am I, send me; and the hard commission to a people who will not turn, ending with the holy seed as a stump.

units.label: The vision of the LORD
units.note: high and exalted, holy, holy, holy

verses.text: In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord seated on a throne, high and exalted; and the train of His robe filled the temple.
Above Him stood {{seraphim|seraphim}}, each having six wings: With two wings they covered their faces, with two they covered their feet, and with two they were flying.

And they were calling out to one another: 
“{{qadosh2|Holy}}, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory.”
At the sound of their voices the doorposts and thresholds shook, and the temple was filled with smoke.

units.label: Ruin and cleansing
units.note: a man of unclean lips touched by a burning coal

verses.text:
Then I said: 
“Woe is me, for I am ruined, because I am a man of unclean lips dwelling among a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Hosts.”
Then one of the seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a glowing coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar.

And with it he touched my mouth and said: 
“Now that this has touched your lips, your {{avon|iniquity}} is removed 
and your sin is atoned for.”

Then I heard the voice of the Lord saying: 
“Whom shall I send? Who will go for Us?” 
And I said: 
“Here am I. Send me!”

units.label: The hard commission
units.note: a hardened people and a holy stump

verses.text:
Make the hearts of this people calloused; deafen their ears and close their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, 
understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed. ”

Then I asked: 
“How long, O Lord?” 
And He replied: 
“Until the cities lie ruined 
and without inhabitant, 
until the houses are left unoccupied and the land is desolate and ravaged,
until the LORD has driven men far away and the land is utterly forsaken.
And though a tenth remains in the land, it will be burned again. As the terebinth and oak leave stumps when felled, so the {{zera_qadosh|holy seed}} will be a stump in the land.”

seraphim.gloss: Burning ones, from a root meaning to burn. These fiery attendants of God's throne, mentioned only here in the Old Testament by this name, cover their own faces and feet even in God's presence, modeling the appropriate response of reverent creatures before the thrice-holy LORD.

qadosh2.gloss: Holy, set apart, utterly other. The threefold repetition, holy, holy, holy, is the only attribute in Scripture repeated three times for emphasis, the highest possible superlative in Hebrew, and it becomes the defining vision behind Isaiah's favorite title for God, the Holy One of Israel.

avon.gloss: Iniquity, guilt, the twisted bent of sin along with its consequence. The coal from the altar removes Isaiah's avon and atones for his sin, a picture of cleansing that requires contact with the altar, foreshadowing the atonement that would finally deal with guilt fully at the cross.

zera_qadosh.gloss: Holy seed, the tiny remnant surviving even the final felling of the nation, like a stump left after a tree is cut down. This stump image directly anticipates Isaiah 11:1, where a shoot springs from the stump of Jesse, tying the surviving remnant to the coming Messiah.

basic.context: In the year King Uzziah died, a moment of national uncertainty, Isaiah is given an overwhelming vision of the LORD enthroned in the temple, surrounded by seraphim crying holy, holy, holy. Undone by his own sinfulness in the presence of such purity, Isaiah is cleansed by a coal from the altar and then volunteers to be sent, only to receive a hard commission: his preaching will actually harden the people further, until judgment falls and only a small, holy remnant survives like a stump after a tree is felled.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real, personal commissioning vision that also functions programmatically for the entire book, explaining why Isaiah's message would be so widely rejected. The most difficult verses are 9-10, where God seems to command hardening rather than repentance; the honest answer, confirmed by how all four Gospels and Acts quote this passage, is that persistent rejection of truth eventually becomes itself a form of judicial hardening, not that God arbitrarily prevents willing repentance.
basic.originalLanguages: The seraphim, burning ones, cover their own faces before the thrice-repeated qadosh, holy, the highest superlative in Hebrew, used nowhere else of any other attribute of God. Isaiah's avon, iniquity, is removed by contact with the altar's coal, and the surviving remnant is called the zera qadosh, the holy seed, a stump image picked up again in Isaiah 11:1 where a shoot springs from the stump of Jesse.
basic.typology: The burning coal from the altar that removes Isaiah's guilt anticipates the full and final atonement accomplished at the cross, where contact with the true altar of sacrifice, Christ Himself, cleanses sin completely. The stump left after felling, the holy seed, directly anticipates the shoot from the stump of Jesse in Isaiah 11:1, the Messiah who springs from a remnant nearly cut off entirely.
basic.christ: John 12:39-41 explicitly says Isaiah saw Christ's glory when he saw the LORD high and exalted, identifying the enthroned figure of Isaiah 6 with Jesus Himself. Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:9-10 to explain why He teaches in parables, Matthew 13:14-15, and the same hardening pattern explains Israel's response to the gospel in Acts 28:26-27 and Romans 11:8, showing that the hardening of Isaiah's day previews and continues into the rejection of Christ.
basic.god: God is holy beyond ordinary human categories, so much so that even sinless angelic beings veil themselves before Him, yet He is also the God who initiates cleansing for a ruined sinner who never could have approached Him on his own. His justice can give a people over to the hardness they have chosen, while His mercy always preserves a holy seed through whom hope continues.
basic.crossReferences: John 12:39-41 identifies the enthroned LORD Isaiah saw as Christ in His glory. Matthew 13:14-15 has Jesus quote this very passage to explain the purpose of His parables. Acts 28:26-27 applies the same hardening text to Israel's rejection of the gospel through Paul. Romans 11:8 draws on this same theme of a spirit of stupor as part of God's larger, ultimately merciful purposes for Israel and the nations.
basic.oneStory: Isaiah 6 shows the pattern that runs through the whole Bible: an encounter with the holy God exposes human sin, but that same God provides cleansing and calls the cleansed into mission, even when that mission will be met with hardened rejection. The holy seed left as a stump carries the story forward to Christ, the shoot who rises from apparent devastation to bring the ultimate atonement Isaiah's coal could only foreshadow.

context.literary:
The chapter moves like a descent and an ascent. It begins high, with the King on His throne and the seraphim above Him, verses 1 to 4. It drops to the floor with Isaiah's cry of ruin in verse 5, then rises again with the flying coal and the voice of verse 8. The commission of verses 9 to 13 is the longest section and the hardest, and it is carried by a short exchange: 'How long, O Lord?' and the answer. The vision is told entirely in the first person, in Isaiah's own voice.

The passage is tied together by a few repeated words. 'Holy' comes three times from the seraphim, and the same root returns in the last line, where the 'holy seed' is the stump, verse 13, so the song of verse 3 and the survivors of verse 13 are bracketed by one word. 'Lips' appears in verses 5 and 7, the mouth that is unclean and the mouth that is touched, and then Isaiah is sent to speak. 'See' and 'hear' in verses 9 and 10 turn the senses Isaiah used in verses 1 to 8 into the senses the people lack. 'Full' marks the glory that fills the earth in verse 3 and the train of the robe that fills the temple in verse 1, while verse 11 describes a land emptied of inhabitants.

The placement of the chapter matters. Chapters 1 to 5 are a sustained indictment, and chapter 6 explains the preacher who delivered it, and the sentence he would meet. Chapters 7 and 8 then show the hardening in action in the person of King Ahaz. The call is the hinge between the charge sheet and the long story of judgment and hope, and its last word, the holy seed, plants the hope that Isaiah 11:1 will grow.
context.historical:
The date is the year of King Uzziah's death, about 740 BC. Uzziah had reigned some fifty years and was remembered as a strong king, but 2 Chronicles 26:16-21 records that in his strength 'his arrogance led to his own destruction.' He entered the temple to burn incense, which only priests might do, and was struck with leprosy, living the rest of his days apart. The scene in Isaiah 6 reads as a deliberate contrast. A human king who tried to enter the holy place was driven out as unclean; the true King sits enthroned in that very place, and the man who stands in His presence is unclean and is cleansed by God's own act.

The temple setting is also plain. The smoke of verse 4 recalls the cloud that filled Solomon's temple so that the priests could not stand, 1 Kings 8:10-11, and the shaking of the thresholds recalls Sinai, Exodus 19:18. The altar from which the coal is taken is the altar of incense or of sacrifice; Leviticus 16:12-13 describes the high priest taking burning coals from the altar once a year on the Day of Atonement, so that the cloud of incense would shield him from death. The text does not say which altar Isaiah sees, but its fire was the fire of atonement.

Seraphim are not mentioned elsewhere as heavenly attendants in the Old Testament, though the word is used of fiery serpents, Numbers 21:6, and of flying serpents in Isaiah 14:29 and 30:6, so some think the idea of fire and of guardianship lies behind the name.

The nation at the time was prosperous and religiously active, as chapters 1 and 5 show. The commission to 'this people' is given at the peak of the nation's comfort, with Assyria, the instrument of the 'ruined cities' of verse 11, still a generation away from reaching Judah in force.
context.canonical:
Isaiah's vision belongs to a small family of throne room scenes. Micaiah saw the LORD on His throne with the host of heaven standing by, 1 Kings 22:19-23. Ezekiel saw a throne with the likeness of a man upon it, Ezekiel 1:26-28, and in Ezekiel 10:1-4 the man clothed in linen is told to take burning coals from among the cherubim, a link to Isaiah's coal. John saw the throne in Revelation 4:2-8, and the four living creatures there do not rest from the cry 'Holy, holy, holy,' which is Isaiah 6:3 sung in heaven.

The commissions of Moses, Jeremiah and Ezekiel follow a pattern that Isaiah 6 shares: a revelation, a sense of inadequacy, an assurance, a mission. Moses says he is slow of speech and the LORD asks, 'Who gave man his mouth?' Exodus 4:10-12. Jeremiah protests that he is only a child and the LORD touches his mouth and puts His words there, Jeremiah 1:6-10. Isaiah's unclean lips and the cleansing coal are the same event from another angle. Ezekiel is sent 'to a rebellious nation,' Ezekiel 2:3-7, and told to speak whether they listen or refuse.

The hardening of verses 9 and 10 is one of the most quoted texts in the New Testament. Jesus applies it to the response to His parables, Matthew 13:10-15 and Mark 4:10-12. John uses it to explain why the signs did not produce faith, John 12:37-41, and states that 'Isaiah said these things because he saw Jesus' glory.' Paul ends the book of Acts with it, Acts 28:25-27, and uses it in Romans 11:7-8. The remnant theme of verse 13 is picked up in Isaiah 10:20-23, quoted in Romans 9:27-29, and the stump and shoot of Isaiah 11:1 are its fulfilment.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah wanted his hearers to know why the prophet who had just spoken in chapters 1 to 5 was not the author of his own message and why the message would not be popular. By telling of the vision, he anchors his authority in the throne room rather than in his own character. He is not a self appointed critic of the nation; he is a man who saw the King and was sent.

He also wanted Judah to learn the right order of things. Holiness comes first, then the exposure of sin, then the cleansing that is entirely God's doing, and only then the sending. The prophet's own confession, 'I am a man of unclean lips dwelling among a people of unclean lips,' places him alongside his listeners rather than above them. He does not preach from a position of cleanliness, but from a position of mercy received.

The commission of verses 9 and 10 is meant to prepare the faithful for the coming rejection. A people who have been hearing the prophets for a generation and still do not turn will not be won by a better sermon. The word 'How long?' in verse 11 shows that Isaiah himself shrank from the answer, and the answer is not left at ruin. A tenth, then a stump, then a holy seed. The message to those who would listen, then and later, was that the judgment would be real but not the end of the story.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The vision is a record of one man's unique commission, not a pattern that every believer should expect to repeat. Nothing in the chapter tells us to look for seraphim or a coal. Nor is the hardening of verses 9 and 10 a method for preachers, as if the aim of preaching were to make hearers deaf. It is a description of what Isaiah's ministry would in fact produce, given the people he was sent to.

What the passage does teach by example is the order of response before the holy God. Isaiah does not defend himself, minimize his sin, or offer a bargain. He confesses, receives cleansing he could not give himself, and then, when the call comes, says 'Here am I. Send me!' The New Testament treats confession and God's cleansing in the same order, 1 John 1:7-9. And the New Testament extends the idea of sending to the whole church, Romans 10:14-15, and to the way Christ's followers are sent, John 20:21. The call to 'go' is not limited to prophets, though the hardening forecast belongs to Isaiah's historical task and is not a promise to every messenger.

debates.question: Who hardens in verses 9 and 10: God, the prophet's message, or the people themselves?

views.label: God hardens judicially
views.case: The verbs are imperatives addressed to Isaiah, 'Make the hearts of this people calloused,' and in the vision it is the LORD who commands. John 12:39-40 takes it so: 'He has blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts.' Deuteronomy 29:4 had already said that the LORD 'has not given you a mind to understand, eyes to see, or ears to hear.' On this view God's sovereign judgment confirms a people already in rebellion, as Isaiah 1 and 5 describe.

views.label: The message exposes and the people harden
views.case: Matthew 13:15 and Acts 28:27 follow the Greek version, where the people's own heart 'has grown callous' and they have 'closed their eyes,' so the agent is the people. The Hebrew can be read as an ironic, rhetorical command that describes the result of the preaching more than its purpose. A message that is refused leaves the refuser more resistant.

views.label: Becoming like what you worship
views.case: Psalm 115:4-8 says of idols that they have eyes that cannot see and ears that cannot hear, and of their worshippers, 'Those who make them become like them.' Isaiah 44:18 says the idolaters cannot comprehend because their eyes are shut. On this reading Israel's idolatry has already made them spiritually blind and deaf, and the commission names the result.

debates.bearing: The three views are not strictly exclusive. The text and the New Testament together present a people who refuse and a God who confirms that refusal in judgment, Romans 1:24, while the offer of healing in verse 10 remains in view: 'turn and be healed.' No passage here says that anyone who wished to turn was prevented, and the prophet's task still involves speaking to them.

debates.question: Who is 'Us' in verse 8?

views.label: The heavenly council
views.case: The question 'Who will go for Us?' echoes the assembly around the throne in 1 Kings 22:19-23, where the LORD takes counsel with the host of heaven. The seraphim are present, and the plural includes the LORD and His court. Isaiah is invited to join that council as a messenger.

views.label: A plurality within God
views.case: The shift from 'Whom shall I send?' to 'Who will go for Us?' is within one speaker, and the same plural appears in Genesis 1:26, 'Let Us make man,' and Genesis 11:7. Christians have long seen in these places an early hint of the Trinity, and John 12:41 connects the vision with Christ while Acts 28:25 attributes the words to the Holy Spirit.

views.label: A plural of majesty or of deliberation
views.case: Some take the plural as God speaking of Himself with His court, or as a plural of fullness, without any claim about persons in God.

debates.bearing: Whichever view one holds, the chapter does not say that the seraphim are the senders, and Isaiah responds to the LORD alone. The New Testament, by tying the vision to Christ in John 12:41 and to the Spirit in Acts 28:25, gives Christians a reason to hear the plural as the fuller revelation of God that the later Scriptures bring.

study.originalLanguages:
The seraphim are called by a word from the verb saraph, 'to burn.' They are 'the burning ones,' and the name suits a vision in which fire from the altar purifies. The description of their wings in verse 2 is an act of worship as well as a feature: faces covered, because they cannot look on the King; feet covered, which many take as a modest idiom for the body in the presence of the King; and two wings for flying, which is service. Two thirds of their equipment is for reverence and one third for work.

The phrase 'high and exalted' in verse 1 uses the same two roots, rum and nasa, that appear in the BSB's rendering of Isaiah 52:13, 'He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted.' The same pair of words describes the LORD on His throne and the Servant whose suffering is the subject of chapter 53. John seems to catch this when he writes that Isaiah saw the glory of Jesus, John 12:41, right after quoting Isaiah 53:1 in John 12:38.

The cry of verse 5, 'I am ruined,' is nidmeti. The root can mean to be silent or to be cut off, and the cry is therefore both 'I am silenced' and 'I am destroyed.' The one who was about to speak for God discovers that his own mouth is the problem. The word for 'unclean,' tame, belongs to the vocabulary of the ritual law, used for lepers and for anything unfit for the sanctuary, Leviticus 13:45. The king who had been struck with leprosy in the temple of verse 1 sits behind this word.

In verse 7 the angel says that Isaiah's guilt is 'removed' and his sin 'atoned for.' The second verb is from the root kipper, the same root as the Day of Atonement, and the first verb, sur, means to turn aside or take away. The grammar presents both as accomplished facts, done to him and not by him, and the cleansing is by contact with the altar's fire, not with water.

Isaiah's answer in verse 8, 'Here am I,' is a single Hebrew word, hineni, which is how Abraham answered God in Genesis 22:1, Moses at the bush, Exodus 3:4, and Samuel in the temple, 1 Samuel 3:4. The word 'Send me' is a command form of the verb shalach. He offers himself in the same voice as the earlier men, but unlike Moses and Jeremiah he does not protest.

In verse 9 the people are to hear 'continually,' with a repeated form of the same verb in Hebrew, 'hearing, hear,' and 'seeing, see.' The structure is a related intensive pairing of a command with its infinitive, the kind of doubling that Genesis 2:17 also uses, so the sentence is a way of saying 'keep on hearing' without understanding. In verse 10 the Hebrew verb behind 'make calloused' is a form of shamen, 'to be fat,' so the heart is made thick or insensitive.

The Septuagint of verses 9 and 10 is different, as the BSB footnote notes: it makes the heart of the people the subject, 'this people's heart has grown callous.' Matthew and Acts follow that form. The last phrase of verse 13 is compressed enough that translators differ over how to render it, but all agree that the holy seed is what the felled tree leaves behind.

typology.type: The coal from the altar, Isaiah 6:6-7
typology.fulfillment: A burning coal from the altar touches the lips of a man who could not cleanse himself. The altar was where blood and fire dealt with sin, Leviticus 16:12-13, and the correspondence is that cleansing comes from God's side of the altar. In the New Testament that altar is the cross: 'without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness,' Hebrews 9:22, and the blood of Jesus 'cleanses us from all sin,' 1 John 1:7. The escalation is that Isaiah was cleansed by a touch in a vision, while believers are cleansed by Christ's once for all offering, Hebrews 9:26. The type falls short because the coal cleansed only for the task of one prophet, and Christ's offering cleanses a people forever.

typology.type: The enthroned King in the temple, Isaiah 6:1
typology.fulfillment: The King seated in the temple, with the train of His robe filling it, is a picture of God's rule and presence among His people. John tells us that Isaiah saw Christ's glory, John 12:41, and the Word who 'made His dwelling among us' is the one in whom 'we have seen His glory,' John 1:14. The Servant who is 'lifted up' in Isaiah 52:13 and Jesus's own words 'when I am lifted up from the earth,' John 12:32, take up the same phrase. The type points beyond a temple building to a person, and the pattern breaks at one point: Isaiah could stand in the vision only because he was cleansed, while Christ is the one who makes that standing possible, Hebrews 10:19-22.

'Whom shall I send?' is answered by a prophet whose lips have been cleansed. The sending finds its fullest answer in the Son, who says in the synagogue, 'The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me,' quoting Isaiah 61:1 and applying it to Himself, Luke 4:18-21. Jesus then sends His disciples as the Father sent Him, John 20:21. Paul asks how anyone can preach unless they are sent, Romans 10:15. The type falls short in that Isaiah was a sinner who needed cleansing before he could go, whereas Christ goes sinless.

typology.type: The stump and the holy seed, Isaiah 6:13
typology.fulfillment: A felled tree leaves a stump, and in that stump a seed of holiness remains. Isaiah 11:1 develops the picture: 'a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse.' The cut down family of David is the stump, and the shoot is the Messiah. Paul says that in the same way there is 'a remnant chosen by grace,' Romans 11:5, and in Revelation 22:16 Jesus says, 'I am the Root and the Offspring of David.' The type stops short in this: the stump in Isaiah's day was the surviving believing Israel, while the full fulfilment is a single Person who then gathers a people.

study.christ:
The most direct link is the one John makes. After telling how the signs of Jesus failed to produce faith, he quotes Isaiah 6:10 and adds, 'Isaiah said these things because he saw Jesus' glory and spoke about Him,' John 12:41. John does not say that Isaiah saw a vision of someone else who was like Jesus; he says Isaiah saw the glory of Jesus. This means that the 'Lord seated on a throne, high and exalted' was, in the Christian reading, the pre-incarnate Son. It is a strong claim, and John expects his readers to accept it without further argument, because it rests on the way the Gospel has already identified Christ as the Word who was with God and was God, John 1:1, and whose glory the disciples saw, John 1:14.

The chapter leads to Christ also by the hardening. All four Gospels and Acts quote Isaiah 6:9-10. Jesus applies it to His parables, Matthew 13:13-15, in the setting of a rejection that was already underway. John applies it to the signs, John 12:37-40. Paul applies it to the Jewish leaders in Rome, Acts 28:25-27. In each case the pattern Isaiah faced reappears: a clear word from God, a mixed response, and a sorrowful reading of the refusal as what Scripture had said it would be. The prophet is told to preach to the end, and so is the one greater than Isaiah.

The cleansing links to Christ by contrast and by fulfilment. Isaiah's lips are touched by a coal brought by an angel; the sinner today is cleansed by the blood of Jesus, 1 John 1:7. The man who said 'I am ruined' is the man whom God makes able to stand. In the same way the writer of Hebrews says that believers may now draw near the Most Holy Place with confidence, Hebrews 10:19-22, because of the sacrifice of Christ.

The last line points to Christ by promise. The holy seed that remains as a stump is the first hint of what Isaiah 11:1 states plainly, a shoot from the stump of Jesse. Jesus is that shoot, and in Revelation 22:16 He calls Himself 'the Root and the Offspring of David.' Even in the hardest verses of the book the story is not left in the ruin of the cut down tree.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The seraphim, the tongs and the coal are not codes for the details of the gospel, and the passage does not describe the cross. What the chapter provides is a vision of the holy King, a sinner made fit to stand before Him by God's own act, and a promise of life from a stump. The New Testament authors take up each of these and find them in Christ.
study.god:
The chapter's central statement about God is the threefold 'Holy' of verse 3, and the way the chapter surrounds it. The triple form is the way Hebrew expresses the highest degree, and the seraphim cry it to one another without ceasing. Holiness here is not a single attribute among many; it is the character of the one who reigns. It is both His moral purity and the otherness that makes Him other than everything He has made. The very beings who burn with fire cover their faces and their feet. The shaking of the doorposts and the smoke tell us that the building itself responds to His voice.

He is King. The first thing Isaiah sees is a throne, and he will say the title in verse 5: 'my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Hosts.' The date given in verse 1, the death of an earthly king, is the quiet comment. Thrones come and go in Judah, and this one does not. The 'hosts' of the divine name are the armies of heaven, so this King is not short of servants.

He is the God whose glory fills the earth. The seraphim say that 'all the earth is full of His glory,' and the passing time of verse 11 will empty the cities of their people. The glory is not tied to the temple, though the temple is where Isaiah sees it. It is the fullness of what God is, shown through the whole creation, and the people who cannot see it are those who cannot see anything at all, verse 10.

He is the one who cleanses, and He does it entirely from His side. Isaiah offers nothing: no vow, no sacrifice, no argument. The seraph brings the coal, and the declaration of forgiveness is made by the angel on God's authority. God's holiness is not softened to let Isaiah in; the sin is dealt with by fire, and God's holiness is the source of the cleansing as well as the reason it is needed.

He is the God who calls. The question of verse 8, 'Whom shall I send?', does not suggest that the LORD cannot act without a messenger. It shows that He chooses to bring His people into His work, and that He asks a cleansed man for his willing yes. The commission itself reveals His sovereignty over what happens to a message after it is delivered, and His justice in confirming a refusal.

He is also the God who keeps a remnant. Verse 13 does not stop at the burning. A tenth, burned again, still leaves a stump, and the stump holds a holy seed. The God of verse 11 who lays cities waste is the same God who preserves a seed for His own purpose. Holy wrath and holy faithfulness are held together in one verse.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to begin where Isaiah began, with who God is, before we ask what we are to do. Its order is vision, confession, cleansing, call. The song of the seraphim is the template for Christian worship, and its right result is a willingness to be sent.

crossReferences.note: The story of Uzziah's pride and leprosy explains the date of Isaiah 6:1. A king who went into the temple unauthorised was struck unclean and shut out; Isaiah, unclean by his own confession, is welcomed and cleansed by the true King. The two scenes help each other, one showing the danger of approaching without consecration, the other its remedy.

Micaiah sees the LORD on His throne with the host of heaven standing by, and hears the LORD ask who will go. It is the nearest Old Testament parallel to the council scene behind Isaiah 6:8, and it shows that a prophet's word is rooted in what he has seen of the heavenly court.

Jeremiah protests that he is only a child, and the LORD touches his mouth and puts His words there. Like Isaiah's coal, this is a physical sign at the mouth that the message is God's own. Both prophets are sent to nations and cities that will not listen, and both are told not to be afraid.

Ezekiel sees the likeness of a throne and a figure like a man upon it, with fire and brilliant light. Like Isaiah, he falls before it and is then commissioned to speak to a rebellious people, Ezekiel 2:3-7. The two visions show how God's throne appears to His prophets at the two ends of Judah's decline.

John sees a throne in heaven and creatures who never cease to say, 'Holy, holy, holy.' The song Isaiah heard in the temple is taken up in the heavenly worship of the last book. It shows that the vision was not a private oddity but a glimpse of what goes on before the throne.

John quotes Isaiah 6:10 to explain why the signs of Jesus did not produce faith, and adds that Isaiah said this because 'he saw Jesus' glory and spoke about Him.' It is the New Testament's decisive statement that the King of Isaiah 6 is Christ.

Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:9-10 to explain why He teaches in parables, using the Greek form where the people's own heart has grown callous. He then says to the disciples, 'blessed are your eyes because they see.' The hardening forecast to Isaiah is happening again in Galilee, and the faithful remnant is those who see.

Paul ends the book of Acts with the Isaiah 6 passage, saying 'The Holy Spirit was right when He spoke to your fathers through Isaiah.' It shows that the apostles read the hardening of the Jewish leaders as the same pattern, and that the Spirit is the one who spoke through the prophet.

A shoot springs from the stump of Jesse. This is the fulfilment of the 'holy seed' stump in Isaiah 6:13: where the earlier chapter leaves a felled tree, this one gives the new growth. It shows that the end of Isaiah 6 is a pause, not a full stop.

The remnant that returns to 'the Mighty God' answers the tenth that remains in Isaiah 6:13, and Isaiah's son Shear-jashub, 'a remnant will return,' gives the promise a name. Paul quotes these verses in Romans 9:27-29 for the remnant chosen by grace.

The Servant is 'raised and lifted up and highly exalted,' using the same pair of words that describe the LORD on His throne in Isaiah 6:1. The link suggests that the exaltation of the Servant is the manifestation of the LORD's own glory, and John treats the two passages together in John 12:38-41.

The idols have eyes, ears and mouths that do not work, and 'those who make them become like them.' The verse is often brought alongside Isaiah 6:9-10, because the people who worship what cannot see or hear become unable to see or hear themselves. It offers a way to understand the hardening as a result of what Israel loved.

study.oneStory:
Isaiah 6 answers a question that has been building since Genesis 3. Adam and Eve hid from God's presence, and the way back was barred by cherubim and a flaming sword, Genesis 3:24. In Isaiah's vision a man comes into that presence, and the fire that guards the way becomes the fire that cleanses. The seraphim carry the burning in which God's holiness is both the barrier and the remedy. The point is not that holiness has relaxed but that God has provided what holiness requires.

The chapter then carries on the story of calling. Abraham was called to be a blessing to all nations, Genesis 12:2-3, and Israel was meant to be a kingdom of priests, Exodus 19:6. In Isaiah's day the nation that was supposed to be a light to the others cannot see, and the prophet is sent to say so. The commission shows the gap between what Israel was called to be and what Israel had become, and it prepares the exile that the next chapters describe.

What follows in Isaiah deepens both sides. The hardening shapes the story of Ahaz in chapters 7 and 8, and the remnant, the tenth and the stump, begins to grow into the promise of the shoot in chapter 11, the servant songs, and the new Zion of the last chapters. The sending that Isaiah accepted, 'Send me,' becomes the pattern of the whole prophetic line, and every later prophet stands in a throne room scene of his own.

The New Testament brings it to its centre. John reads the vision as the glory of Christ, and the hardening is seen again in His ministry, John 12:37-41. Yet the same Gospel records the believing remnant, and the cleansing that Isaiah received at the altar is offered to everyone through the blood of Jesus, 1 John 1:7. The sending is extended from one prophet to the whole church, Matthew 28:19-20 and John 20:21.

In the new creation the song is finished. John hears the same cry, 'Holy, holy, holy,' around the throne, Revelation 4:8, and the people who could not see or hear in Isaiah's day will see 'His face,' Revelation 22:4. The temple that Isaiah's vision filled with smoke is replaced by a city where there is no temple, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. The man who cried 'Woe is me' is among those who stand before the throne, with nothing to hide.

sermon.title: Holy, Holy, Holy Is the Lord of Hosts
sermon.why: Piper works directly through Isaiah 6:1-8, drawing out the overwhelming holiness of God, Isaiah's ruin and cleansing, and the pattern of true calling that flows from a genuine vision of God's glory, exactly the movement this study traces.

quiz.q: What is significant about the seraphim covering their faces and feet even in God's presence?

options.text: It models the appropriate reverence and creaturely humility even sinless beings owe to the thrice-holy God.
options.note: If unfallen angels veil themselves before God's holiness, it heightens the weight of Isaiah's own unworthiness as a sinful man.

options.text: It shows the seraphim were ashamed of their own sin.
options.note: Seraphim are not depicted as sinful; their veiling expresses reverence, not guilt.

options.text: It is simply a description of their physical anatomy with no theological meaning.
options.note: The detail carries clear theological weight about appropriate creaturely response to divine holiness.

options.text: It shows they were hiding from an enemy.
options.note: The context is worship and reverence before God's throne, not fear of an external enemy.

quiz.q: Why does Isaiah cry, 'Woe is me, for I am ruined,' upon seeing the LORD?

options.text: The vision of God's absolute holiness exposed his own uncleanness and that of his people with unbearable clarity.
options.note: Genuine encounter with holiness produces genuine conviction of sin, the pattern seen elsewhere in Scripture.

options.text: He was physically injured by the smoke in the temple.
options.note: His ruin is moral and spiritual, explicitly tied to his unclean lips, not a physical injury.

options.text: He was afraid of losing his prophetic office.
options.note: His concern is his own sinfulness before a holy God, not job security.

options.text: He doubted whether the vision was real.
options.note: Isaiah does not question the vision's reality; he responds with immediate, genuine conviction of sin.

quiz.q: What does the burning coal from the altar accomplish in verse 7?

options.text: It removes Isaiah's iniquity and atones for his sin, cleansing him to be able to serve.
options.note: The cleansing comes through contact with the altar, foreshadowing atonement accomplished at the cross.

options.text: It grants Isaiah supernatural physical strength.
options.note: The stated effect is moral and spiritual cleansing, not physical enhancement.

options.text: It punishes Isaiah for his confession.
options.note: The coal brings cleansing and atonement, not punishment; Isaiah's confession is met with grace.

options.text: It silences Isaiah so he cannot speak further.
options.note: The coal touches his lips to cleanse them, not to silence him; he immediately speaks again in verse 8.

quiz.q: How should the hard commission in verses 9-10 be understood?

options.text: As describing the certain, deserved hardening that follows a people's persistent, prior rejection of God's word.
options.note: The New Testament's own use of this text, Acts 28:26-27, treats it as describing judicial hardening after sustained unbelief.

options.text: As proof that God arbitrarily prevents anyone from ever repenting.
options.note: This misreads the passage as removing all human responsibility, contrary to how the New Testament applies it.

options.text: As a command Isaiah refused to obey.
options.note: Isaiah accepts and carries out this commission; there is no indication of refusal.

options.text: As applying only to Isaiah's original eighth century audience, with no later significance.
options.note: The New Testament explicitly reapplies this text to responses to Jesus and the apostolic gospel, showing ongoing significance.

quiz.q: What does the closing image of the holy seed as a stump, verse 13, anticipate?

options.text: The shoot that will spring from the stump of Jesse in Isaiah 11:1, ultimately fulfilled in Christ.
options.note: The stump and shoot imagery directly links this remnant promise to the coming Messiah.

options.text: The complete and final destruction of Israel with no future hope.
options.note: A stump, unlike total destruction, implies the possibility of new growth, a deliberate note of hope.

options.text: A literal agricultural policy for replanting trees.
options.note: The stump is a symbolic image for a surviving remnant, not literal forestry instruction.

options.text: The restoration of the ten northern tribes specifically.
options.note: The holy seed and stump imagery is a broader remnant motif, developed messianically rather than tied to one specific tribal restoration.

questions: Isaiah's vision of God's holiness immediately exposed his own sinfulness. When was the last time you had a real, humbling encounter with who God actually is, rather than a comfortable idea of Him?
Isaiah did not clean himself up before God acted; the coal came to him. Where do you still try to make yourself presentable to God before letting Him cleanse you?
Isaiah's response to being cleansed was immediate availability: here am I, send me. What is God asking of you right now that you have been slow to volunteer for?
Isaiah was sent to a people who would not listen, yet he still went. Where do you need to remain faithful to obey God even when the response to your obedience may be resistance rather than success?

Even in devastating judgment, God preserved a holy seed. Where in your own life or circumstances do you need to trust that God is preserving something for future growth, even when everything visible looks like a stump?

translationNotes.note: Seraphim, saraph in the singular, means burning ones and appears elsewhere in the Old Testament describing fiery serpents, Numbers 21:6-8; here the term describes radiant, fiery heavenly attendants rather than serpentine beings.

The Hebrew imperatives, make the hearts of this people calloused, are debated between an active causative sense, God actively hardens, and a resultative sense describing what Isaiah's preaching will, in effect, produce among a people already resistant.

'Holy seed' is a striking phrase used elsewhere only in Ezra 9:2 for post-exilic Israel; here it names the small surviving remnant as itself sacred, set apart for God's ongoing purposes despite catastrophic judgment.
